southeast-asia.tagline: Archipelagos, super-apps, and the missing premium water tier.
southeast-asia.summary: Southeast Asia is the world's densest archipelagic mobility market: Indonesia's 17,000 islands, Thailand's island chains, Malaysia's cross-border corridors, the Philippines' airport-to-resort hops, and Singapore's regulator-led clean-harbour push. Super-apps already own last-mile demand — the water leg is the premium tier still sold by diesel ferry and wet speedboat. Explore clusters, cities, and sealed corridors on Navier Atlas.
southeast-asia.why_marine_mobility: No single country tells the Southeast Asian story, because the region IS water: Indonesia alone spans more than 17,000 islands, and the Philippines, Thailand, and Malaysia each run their tourism and daily life across straits, gulfs, and archipelagos. Today that water leg is the weakest link — diesel ferries that are slow and weather-bound, or wet, loud speedboats with no schedule. Super-apps already own how the region books a ride; the premium water tier between island and mainland is the piece still missing.

demand_signals.label: Super-app demand already at the dock
demand_signals.note: Grab, Gojek, and their peers move tens of millions of daily trips. The handoff from a booked car to the boat is where the experience breaks — exactly the seam a clean, scheduled foiling leg closes.

demand_signals.label: Archipelago tourism at scale
demand_signals.note: Bali, Phuket, Boracay, El Nido, Komodo and dozens more pull global visitor volumes whose first and last impression is the transfer boat.

demand_signals.label: Island life depends on the crossing
demand_signals.note: For millions, the ferry isn't a holiday — it's the commute, the hospital run, the supply line. Reliability and weather tolerance are not luxuries here.

use_cases.title: Resort and island gateway transfers
use_cases.body: Airport-to-island and island-to-island legs — Bali–Lombok, Phuket–Krabi, Caticlan–Boracay — run today on ferries and speedboats. A quiet, stable foiling shuttle turns the worst part of the trip into a highlight.

use_cases.title: The water leg inside the app
use_cases.body: A foiling corridor booked in the same app as the car and the scooter — one journey, one receipt — extends a super-app's reach onto water it cannot serve today.

use_cases.title: Cross-border and commuter corridors
use_cases.body: Singapore–Desaru and Sabah–Brunei show the cross-border pattern: a short open-water hop that road and bridge make slow, where a scheduled premium boat is simply faster.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The dense inter-island mesh — Bali–Lombok, the Andaman and Gulf-of-Thailand crossings, the Visayas corridors — sits squarely in Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band: quiet, zero-emission, marina-to-marina.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The long trunks — Lombok–Komodo, Phuket–Langkawi, mainland-to-far-archipelago runs — extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range, opening corridors no electric ferry can reach.

signature_routes.label: Bali ↔ Lombok — the headline resort crossing
Lombok ↔ Komodo — the eastern long-range expedition trunk
Phuket ↔ Krabi — the marquee Andaman crossing
Manila → Palawan (El Nido / Coron / Amanpulo) — the national long-range hero
Singapore → Desaru Coast — the cross-border Johor Strait hop

southeast-asia.transit_planning: For a super-app or a tourism authority: Southeast Asia is the clearest case for a premium water tier layered on existing demand. The cars and scooters are booked; the islands are the destination; only the crossing is unsolved. A foiling mesh slots into the app and the dock that already exist.
southeast-asia.competitive_landscape: Today the water leg splits between public ferries (cheap, slow, weather-limited) and private speedboats (fast, expensive, unscheduled, noisy). Neither is premium-reliable. Electric-hydrofoil mobility occupies the empty middle — scheduled, quiet, and stable in chop.
southeast-asia.seasonality: Monsoon timing differs by coast — Thailand's Andaman and Gulf run opposite seasons, and Indonesia's east dries as the west wets — so a regional operator can chase calm water across the calendar rather than shutting down.

mena.tagline: Gulf islands, Red Sea resorts, and cross-emirate water mobility.
mena.summary: The Middle East combines captive resort islands, congested coastal cities, and ambitious national mobility programs across the Gulf, the Red Sea, and the Levant. From the UAE's harbour-craft mandates to Red Sea gateway resorts and cross-emirate metro hops, marine mobility is the premium overlay super-apps and hospitality groups are still assembling by road and helicopter.
mena.why_marine_mobility: The Middle East pairs some of the world's most ambitious waterfront building programs with congested coastal cities and captive resort islands across the Gulf, the Red Sea, and the Levant. Gulf metros are minutes apart by water yet an hour by road; Red Sea and giga-project resorts are designed around arrival by sea; and the Gulf of Aqaba already prices a premium cross-water transfer. Marine mobility is the overlay these programs are still assembling by road, helicopter, and conventional craft.

demand_signals.label: Gulf metros built on the water's edge
demand_signals.note: Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha and Manama ring their populations around marinas, islands, and corniches — short water lines that today lose to congested causeways.

demand_signals.label: Giga-project resorts arrive by sea
demand_signals.note: Red Sea Global, NEOM, The Pearl and Lusail are designed for water arrival; a clean, fast hydrofoil is the on-brand transfer their guests expect.

demand_signals.label: Cross-border Gulf and Red Sea hops
demand_signals.note: Muscat–Fujairah, Eastern Province–Bahrain, and Sharm–NEOM are short cross-water legs that road routing makes long.

use_cases.title: Cross-emirate and cross-city commuting
use_cases.body: Dubai–Abu Dhabi and Doha–Lusail are the headline metro-to-metro water corridors — a quiet foiling line that beats the highway at peak.

use_cases.title: Resort and island gateway transfers
use_cases.body: Doha–The Pearl, Red Sea Global–NEOM, and Muscat's resort coast turn the guest transfer into part of the experience rather than a logistics problem.

use_cases.title: Cross-border Gulf and Aqaba corridors
use_cases.body: Sharm–NEOM and Eastern Province–Manama show the cross-border opportunity: short open-water hops where a scheduled premium boat replaces a long land detour.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Intra-metro and resort legs — Dubai–Abu Dhabi, Doha–The Pearl, the UAE east coast — fit Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band, ideal for the region's harbour-craft and clean-mobility mandates.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The giga-project trunks — Red Sea Global–NEOM, Muscat–Salalah, cross-Gulf and cross-Aqaba hops — extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range.

signature_routes.label: Dubai ↔ Abu Dhabi — the Gulf metro corridor
Doha Corniche ↔ The Pearl — the all-electric waterfront hop
Red Sea Global ↔ NEOM — the long-range giga-project trunk
Muscat ↔ Salalah — the long-range Dhofar coastal trunk
Sharm El Sheikh ↔ NEOM (Sindalah) — the Gulf of Aqaba cross-border hop

mena.transit_planning: For a Gulf authority or a hospitality developer: the waterfront is already built and the road is already congested. A foiling line is the missing piece that makes island and cross-metro arrival fast, quiet, and on-brand — without new bridges or causeways.
mena.competitive_landscape: Premium transfer today means a chauffeured car stuck in traffic, a helicopter at helicopter cost, or a conventional launch that is slow and fuel-heavy. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is faster than the road, a fraction of the helicopter, and clean enough for the region's sustainability mandates.
mena.seasonality: The Gulf and Red Sea run year-round with a hot, calm summer and mild winter; sea state is rarely a constraint, so corridors operate on a stable all-year schedule.

europe.tagline: Riviera corridors, fjords, and island-hopping at electric range.
europe.summary: Europe's coastal cities, archipelagos, and short-sea corridors are ideal foiling territory: Greek islands, Croatian Adriatic hops, Norwegian fjords, Mediterranean marinas, and cross-channel commuter links where congestion and seasonality already price premium transfer.
europe.why_marine_mobility: Europe's coasts are a near-perfect foiling map: short-sea crossings between islands and headlands that congestion, seasonality, and geography already make premium. The Greek Cyclades, the Croatian Adriatic, the French and Italian rivieras, the Norwegian fjords, and the Baltic and Atlantic city harbours all run heavy water traffic today — much of it on diesel ferries and fast craft that are loud, fuel-heavy, and weather-limited.

demand_signals.label: Mediterranean island tourism at volume
demand_signals.note: The Cyclades, Dalmatia, the Balearics, Capri and the Côte d'Azur draw enormous summer visitor flows whose journeys hinge on the island crossing.

demand_signals.label: Fjord and archipelago lifelines
demand_signals.note: Norway's west coast and the Baltic archipelagos depend on year-round water links where road detours run hours.

demand_signals.label: Harbour commuter corridors
demand_signals.note: Cross-channel and cross-harbour commutes — the Bosphorus, city-to-city Adriatic and North-Sea hops — already carry scheduled premium demand.

use_cases.title: Marquee island crossings
use_cases.body: Split–Hvar, Santorini–Mykonos, Naples–Capri and Nice–Monaco are the iconic legs — exactly where a quiet, stable hydrofoil lifts the experience above the crowded ferry deck.

use_cases.title: Fjord and coastal trunks
use_cases.body: Bergen–Stavanger and the fjord crossings are year-round lifelines where a fast electric leg cuts a long, scenic but slow journey.

use_cases.title: Commuter and cross-water city links
use_cases.body: The Bosphorus and short cross-harbour corridors carry daily commuters who already pay for speed and reliability.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Most European crossings — Cyclades, Dalmatia, Bay of Naples, the Riviera, fjord and harbour legs — sit inside Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band, matching Europe's strict emissions and harbour-noise rules.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The long open-water trunks — Split–Venice, Riviera–Sardinia, Amalfi–Costa Smeralda, Çeşme–Istanbul — reach into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range.

signature_routes.label: Split ↔ Hvar — the marquee Dalmatian crossing
Santorini ↔ Mykonos — the marquee Cyclades crossing
Naples ↔ Capri — the Bay of Naples crossing
Nice ↔ Monaco (Port Hercule) — the iconic Riviera hop
Bergen ↔ Stavanger — the Norwegian west-coast trunk

europe.transit_planning: For a European port city or regional authority: foiling lines decarbonise the busiest tourist and commuter crossings without new infrastructure, and they do it quietly enough to satisfy the strictest harbour and marine-park rules.
europe.competitive_landscape: Conventional fast ferries dominate but are noisy, fuel-heavy, and uncomfortable in chop; private launches are expensive and unscheduled. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is the quiet, stable, emissions-clean upgrade on the same routes.
europe.seasonality: Mediterranean demand peaks May–October and the meltemi and bora winds shape summer scheduling; Atlantic and Baltic corridors run year-round with winter sea-state planning. Stability in chop is a real competitive edge here.

south-asia.tagline: Mega-city rivers, island gateways, and super-app scale.
south-asia.summary: South Asia pairs some of the world's largest urban populations with island and backwater corridors — Kerala's waterways, Sri Lanka's coast, India's Andaman gateway, and Bangladesh's delta geography. Ride-hailing scale meets water surfaces that ferries and roads cannot serve cleanly.
south-asia.why_marine_mobility: South Asia couples some of the planet's largest urban populations with island gateways and backwater geographies that road and conventional ferry serve poorly. India's west coast, Kerala's waterways, the Andamans, the Maldivian atolls, and the Sri Lankan and Seychellois island chains all run on water — and ride-hailing has already taught the region to book mobility on a phone.

demand_signals.label: Resort-atoll transfers at the top of the market
demand_signals.note: The Maldives runs almost entirely on resort transfers — seaplane and launch today — a captive, premium, year-round flow built for a quiet foiling upgrade.

demand_signals.label: Mega-city and backwater corridors
demand_signals.note: Mumbai harbour, Kochi's backwaters, and Goa's coast pair dense demand with water surfaces that roads cannot relieve.

demand_signals.label: Island-nation gateway hops
demand_signals.note: Praslin–La Digue, Mahé–Praslin, and the Andaman gateway are tourist-critical crossings run on conventional ferries today.

use_cases.title: Maldivian resort transfers
use_cases.body: Malé–Soneva Fushi and Malé–Six Senses Laamu are flagship resort legs where a stable, quiet hydrofoil competes directly with the seaplane on comfort and reach.

use_cases.title: West-coast and backwater corridors
use_cases.body: Goa–Mumbai and Kochi–Backwaters pair long-range coastal trunks with dense urban water that a foiling line serves where road cannot.

use_cases.title: Inner-island tourist hops
use_cases.body: Praslin–La Digue and the Andaman gateway are the marquee leisure crossings — short, scenic, and ferry-bound today.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Atoll, backwater, and inner-island legs — Maldivian transfers, Kochi, the Seychelles hops, Mumbai harbour — fit Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The long trunks — Goa–Mumbai, Colombo–Malé, southern-atoll runs — extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range.

Malé (Velana) → Soneva Fushi — the flagship resort transfer
Colombo ↔ Malé — the South Asian regional gateway
Praslin ↔ La Digue — the iconic Seychelles Inner-Islands hop
Kochi ↔ Kerala Backwaters — the heritage-waterway leg

south-asia.transit_planning: For a resort group or a coastal-city authority: South Asia offers both the captive premium market (atoll transfers) and the dense-demand market (mega-city harbours) — a foiling tier serves the top and the middle of the same map.
south-asia.competitive_landscape: Today it is seaplanes and launches at the luxury end (costly, weather-limited) and public ferries at the essential end (slow, crowded). Electric-hydrofoil mobility sits between — faster and quieter than the ferry, cheaper and lower-impact than the seaplane.
south-asia.seasonality: The southwest monsoon (roughly June–September) governs the Indian and Sri Lankan coasts; the Maldives and Seychelles run year-round with monsoon-shifted calm sides — so an operator can follow calm water seasonally.

east-asia.tagline: Island nations, inland seas, and high-frequency coastal demand.
east-asia.summary: East Asia spans Japan's inland sea and Ryukyu chains, Korea's coastal cities, Taiwan's island hops, and Greater China's Pearl River Delta — dense, tech-forward markets where premium water mobility can slot into existing super-app habits. Commuters and visitors already pay for speed and reliability, and much of the heavy short-hop water traffic still runs on slower conventional ferries today.
east-asia.why_marine_mobility: East Asia is a string of island nations and inland seas wrapped around dense, tech-forward cities. Japan's Seto Inland Sea and Ryukyu chain, Korea's southern island sea, Taiwan's Penghu archipelago, and the Pearl River Delta all carry heavy, habitual water traffic — and these are exactly the markets most ready to book a premium water leg on a phone.

demand_signals.label: Inland-sea and island tourism
demand_signals.note: The Seto Inland Sea art islands, Jeju, the Yaeyamas, and Penghu pull strong domestic and regional visitor flows across short crossings.

demand_signals.label: Coastal-city commuter density
demand_signals.note: Pearl River Delta and Korean and Japanese coastal cities concentrate enormous commuter demand on the water's edge.

demand_signals.label: Resort-coast and archipelago hops
demand_signals.note: Jeju's resort coast and the Penghu inter-island links are tourist-critical legs served by conventional ferries today.

use_cases.title: Island-sea trunk corridors
use_cases.body: Busan/Geoje–Jeju and Seto Inland Sea–Tokyo Bay are the long coastal trunks where a fast foiling line reshapes a slow ferry journey.

use_cases.title: Subtropical and archipelago hops
use_cases.body: Ishigaki–Kabira and the Penghu resort legs are short, scenic crossings ideal for a quiet, stable hydrofoil.

use_cases.title: Hallyeo and coastal commuter links
use_cases.body: Busan–Yeosu/Tongyeong and the southern-coast corridors carry mixed commuter and tourist demand on a daily rhythm.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Most East-Asian crossings — Ryukyu hops, Penghu links, Jeju's resort coast, the Hallyeo corridor — sit inside Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The long island-sea trunks — Busan/Geoje–Jeju, Seto Inland Sea–Tokyo Bay — reach into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range.

Busan / Geoje ↔ Jeju — the long-range island-sea trunk
Ishigaki ↔ Kabira Bay — the subtropical Yaeyama hop

east-asia.transit_planning: For a Japanese, Korean, or Taiwanese operator: the demand and the digital habit already exist; a foiling tier decarbonises the busiest island crossings and adds a premium option the conventional ferry cannot match.
east-asia.competitive_landscape: High-speed ferries are well established but loud, fuel-heavy, and rough in swell. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is the quiet, stable, zero-local-emission upgrade on the same proven routes.
east-asia.seasonality: Typhoon season (roughly July–October) shapes summer scheduling across the region; spring and autumn are peak calm-water windows, and the inland seas stay relatively sheltered year-round.

latin-america.tagline: Coastal megacities, Caribbean gateways, and tourism archipelagos.
latin-america.summary: Latin America combines Pacific and Atlantic coastal corridors, Caribbean leisure islands, and congested waterfront cities where a quiet foiling tier unlocks resort transfers and commuter relief without new highway spend. Brazil's Costa Verde, Mexico's Caribbean and Baja coasts, and the Pacific resort bays all carry heavy water traffic on conventional craft that a faster, cleaner tier can upgrade.
latin-america.why_marine_mobility: Latin America wraps Pacific and Atlantic coasts around leisure archipelagos and waterfront cities where a quiet foiling tier unlocks resort transfers and commuter relief without new highway spend. Brazil's Costa Verde, Mexico's Caribbean and Baja coasts, and the Pacific resort bays all run heavy water traffic on conventional craft today.

demand_signals.label: Leisure-archipelago demand
demand_signals.note: Rio's Costa Verde / Ilha Grande, Cancún–Isla Mujeres, and Los Cabos pull strong leisure flows across short, scenic crossings.

demand_signals.label: Waterfront-city corridors
demand_signals.note: Coastal megacities pair dense demand with bays and channels that road traffic clogs.

demand_signals.label: Resort-marina transfers
demand_signals.note: Riviera Nayarit, Los Cabos, and Angra's marinas serve a premium transfer market built for a clean hydrofoil.

use_cases.title: Day-island and leisure crossings
use_cases.body: Cancún–Isla Mujeres and Rio–Ilha Grande are the marquee leisure legs — short crossings where a quiet, stable foiling shuttle outclasses the crowded ferry.

use_cases.title: Resort-marina transfers
use_cases.body: Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta marina legs turn the guest transfer into part of the stay.

use_cases.title: Bay and coastal commuter relief
use_cases.body: Waterfront cities can move people across the bay faster by foiling line than by congested shore road.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Bay, day-island, and resort-marina legs — Cancún–Isla Mujeres, the Costa Verde and Baja hops — sit inside Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer Pacific and Atlantic coastal trunks extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range as corridors mature.

latin-america.transit_planning: For a coastal-city or tourism authority: a foiling tier adds premium leisure transfers and bay-crossing commuter relief on the water that is already the city's front door — no new road needed.
latin-america.competitive_landscape: Diesel ferries and pangas dominate today — affordable but slow, loud, and weather-limited at the leisure end. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is the quiet, reliable premium tier on the same routes.
latin-america.seasonality: The Caribbean and Pacific coasts have a wet/hurricane season (roughly June–November) and a dry, calm high season; an operator schedules premium demand into the calm-water months.

caribbean.tagline: Island-hopping leisure and inter-island essential mobility.
caribbean.summary: The Caribbean is defined by water — resort transfers, inter-island commuters, and cruise-gateway hops where diesel ferries and small aircraft are the only options today. A premium electric-hydrofoil mesh raises reliability and cuts noise across short-sea corridors.
caribbean.why_marine_mobility: The Caribbean is defined by water: resort transfers, inter-island commutes, and cruise-gateway hops where diesel ferries and small aircraft are often the only options. A premium electric-hydrofoil mesh raises reliability and cuts noise across hundreds of short-sea corridors — but the region's sealed hero corridors are still being built, so the network here is shown by its clusters and gateways rather than by marquee routes yet.

demand_signals.label: Island-hopping leisure at scale
demand_signals.note: The Caribbean's economy runs on resort and cruise-gateway transfers across short, scenic crossings.

demand_signals.label: Inter-island lifelines
demand_signals.note: For island communities the inter-island boat is essential infrastructure, not a holiday extra.

demand_signals.label: Private-island and resort transfers
demand_signals.note: High-end resorts and private islands depend on a premium, reliable transfer that conventional craft deliver inconsistently.

use_cases.title: Resort and cruise-gateway transfers
use_cases.body: Short island-to-island and gateway-to-resort legs where a quiet, stable hydrofoil lifts the arrival experience above the diesel ferry.

use_cases.title: Inter-island commuter links
use_cases.body: Daily inter-island travel that conventional ferries serve slowly — a foiling line adds speed and reliability.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The Caribbean's dense short-sea mesh fits Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band — quiet, zero-emission island hops.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer inter-island and cross-channel trunks extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range as corridors are sealed.

caribbean.transit_planning: For a Caribbean tourism authority or resort group: the opportunity is a premium, reliable water mesh across corridors small aircraft and diesel ferries serve today — explore the clusters and gateways below as the sealed corridor map fills in.
caribbean.competitive_landscape: Today it is diesel ferries (cheap, slow, weather-bound) and small aircraft (fast, costly, capacity-limited). Electric-hydrofoil mobility occupies the reliable, quiet premium middle.
caribbean.seasonality: Hurricane season (roughly June–November) shapes scheduling; the December–April dry season is the calm-water peak.

north-america.tagline: Harbour cities, island metros, and coastal congestion relief.
north-america.summary: North America's harbour cities and coastal corridors — from Pacific Northwest islands to the Florida keys, NYC harbour commuting, and Great Lakes gateways — are natural foiling markets where water is faster than gridlocked road. These markets carry heavy ferry and water-taxi volumes today, with commuters and visitors who already pay a premium for the time they save on the water.
north-america.why_marine_mobility: North America's harbour cities and coastal corridors are natural foiling markets where the water is simply faster than gridlocked road. The Pacific Northwest island mesh, the Florida coast and the Bahamas crossing, the Hawaiian channels, and the great harbour cities all carry heavy water traffic — and commuters and visitors who already pay for speed.

demand_signals.label: Harbour-city congestion relief
demand_signals.note: Florida's coast, NYC harbour, and the Salish Sea pair dense demand with road networks that gridlock at peak.

demand_signals.label: Island-channel leisure
demand_signals.note: The Hawaiian inter-island channels and the Bahamas crossing carry strong, premium-priced visitor demand.

demand_signals.label: Island-community lifelines
demand_signals.note: Pacific Northwest and New England island communities depend on year-round water links.

use_cases.body: Palm Beach–Miami and Gulf-coast trunks move commuters faster by water than by congested interstate.

use_cases.title: Island-channel crossings
use_cases.body: Oʻahu–Maui, Honolulu–Kauaʻi, and Miami–Nassau are the marquee channel crossings — long, premium legs where speed and stability matter most.

use_cases.title: Archipelago lifelines
use_cases.body: Salish Sea and San Juan island links are year-round essential corridors a quiet foiling line serves cleanly.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Harbour-commute and short coastal legs — Palm Beach–Miami, the Salish Sea mesh — sit inside Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The open-water channels — Oʻahu–Maui, Miami–Nassau, Tampa–Naples — reach into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range.

north-america.transit_planning: For a US or Canadian harbour authority: a foiling line relieves the most congested waterfront commutes and adds a premium island-channel option, all on water the city already fronts.
north-america.competitive_landscape: Conventional ferries and water taxis are established but slow and fuel-heavy; small aircraft serve the channels at high cost. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is the quiet, fast, clean upgrade across both.
north-america.seasonality: Atlantic hurricane season and Pacific winter storms shape scheduling; summer is the peak calm-water and visitor window across most corridors.

oceania.tagline: Pacific archipelagos and Australasian coastal gateways.
oceania.summary: Oceania spans Australia's harbour cities, New Zealand's coastal corridors, and Pacific island chains where inter-island transport is essential infrastructure and tourism depends on reliable water links. Fiji's Mamanuca and Yasawa groups and French Polynesia's Society Islands run almost entirely on resort and inter-island transfers, much of it on slower conventional vessels today.
oceania.why_marine_mobility: Oceania spans Australasian harbour cities and the Pacific island chains where inter-island transport is essential infrastructure and tourism depends on reliable water links. Fiji's Mamanuca and Yasawa groups and French Polynesia's Society Islands run almost entirely on resort and inter-island transfers today.

oceania.transit_planning: For a Pacific resort group or island authority: a foiling tier upgrades the transfer that defines the visitor experience and strengthens the essential inter-island links communities rely on.
oceania.competitive_landscape: Today it is conventional resort launches and ferries — slow, loud, and weather-limited. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is the quiet, stable, clean premium transfer on the same routes.

africa.tagline: Coastal cities, island states, and emerging super-app corridors.
africa.summary: Africa's coastal megacities, island nations, and lake corridors combine essential mobility demand with rapidly scaling ride-hailing platforms — a greenfield premium water tier for crossings that ferries serve slowly today. From the East African coast to the Indian Ocean islands and the West African waterfronts, dense populations already move heavily by water on conventional craft.
africa.why_marine_mobility: Africa's coastal cities, island states, and lake corridors pair essential-mobility demand with rapidly scaling ride-hailing — a greenfield premium water tier for crossings that ferries serve slowly today. The East African coast, the Indian Ocean islands, and the West African waterfronts all run heavy water traffic on conventional craft.

demand_signals.label: Indian-Ocean island tourism
demand_signals.note: Zanzibar and the East African coast pull strong visitor flows across iconic ferry crossings.

demand_signals.label: Coastal-city and lake corridors
demand_signals.note: Coastal megacities and the great lakes pair dense demand with water surfaces underserved by reliable transport.

demand_signals.label: Ride-hailing scaling on the coast
demand_signals.note: African super-apps and ride-hailing platforms are scaling fast in coastal cities — the water leg is the natural premium extension.

use_cases.title: Island ferry crossings upgraded
use_cases.body: Dar es Salaam–Zanzibar and the Stone Town day-trip hops are iconic, heavily used crossings where a quiet, stable hydrofoil lifts a slow ferry journey.

use_cases.title: Coastal and lake commuter corridors
use_cases.body: Coastal cities and lake gateways can move people faster across the water than around congested shore roads.

use_cases.title: West-African waterfront commuter and gateway legs
use_cases.body: From Dakar's Gorée crossing and Abidjan's Ebrié Lagoon to Lagos's lagoon commute and Luanda's bay, dense waterfront cities pair heavy ride-hailing adoption with water legs that cut congested shore-road detours — the premium foiling line rides on top of demand that already moves by boat.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Island-crossing and coastal legs — Dar es Salaam–Zanzibar, the Stone Town hops — fit Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer coastal and inter-island trunks extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range as corridors are sealed.

africa.transit_planning: For an African coastal authority or super-app: the demand and the digital habit are scaling together; a foiling tier adds a premium, reliable water leg on the busiest crossings without new road or rail.
africa.competitive_landscape: Today it is diesel ferries (cheap, slow, crowded) and informal boats. Electric-hydrofoil mobility is the quiet, reliable premium upgrade on the same well-travelled corridors.
africa.seasonality: The Indian Ocean monsoon (the kaskazi and kusi winds) shapes the East African coast's calendar; an operator schedules premium demand into the calm-water seasons.
africa.regulatory_note: Coastal African markets operate under national maritime and port authorities with varied passenger-ferry licensing; operations are framed domestic-first within each country's territorial waters, coordinated with the local port authority and the scaling ride-hail platform. Cross-border coastal legs are sealed only where bilateral clearance exists.

caspian.tagline: Inland sea corridors between energy and tourism gateways.
caspian.summary: The Caspian basin links Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan coastal cities across the world's largest inland sea, where cross-shore mobility is ferry-dependent and built around energy and trade gateways. The network here is early — represented by its gateway cities rather than sealed hero corridors yet — but the cross-sea geography is a natural fit for a quiet, premium foiling overlay.
caspian.why_marine_mobility: The Caspian basin links Azerbaijan's and Kazakhstan's coastal cities across the world's largest inland sea, where cross-shore mobility is ferry-dependent and built around energy and trade gateways. The network here is early — shown by its gateway cities rather than by sealed hero corridors yet — but the cross-sea geography is a natural fit for a premium foiling overlay.

demand_signals.label: Cross-sea gateway demand
demand_signals.note: Baku, Aktau, and Kuryk anchor energy and trade flows where cross-shore movement is slow and ferry-dependent today.

demand_signals.label: Coastal-city corridors
demand_signals.note: Caspian coastal cities pair concentrated demand with water links that conventional craft serve infrequently.

demand_signals.label: Energy-sector crew and trade movement
demand_signals.note: Baku's offshore energy complex and the Aktau/Kuryk port cluster generate steady crew-transfer and business travel that today rely on road detours and infrequent craft.

use_cases.title: Cross-shore gateway links
use_cases.body: Short cross-water legs between Caspian gateway cities where a fast, reliable foiling line would replace infrequent ferry service.

use_cases.title: Intra-bay and near-shore city legs
use_cases.body: Within Baku Bay and along the Absheron shore, short water legs let riders skip the congested coastal road between the corniche, the White City waterfront, and outlying marinas.

use_cases.title: Caspian waterfront leisure hops
use_cases.body: Baku's boulevard seafront and the Kazakh coast's beach clusters (Kenderli, Kuryk) draw leisure demand that a quiet premium foiling line can serve on calm-water days.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Near-shore and intra-bay Caspian legs fit Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer cross-sea trunks would extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range as corridors are sealed.

caspian.transit_planning: For a Caspian coastal authority: the inland-sea geography concentrates demand on a handful of gateway cities — explore them below as the sealed corridor map develops.
caspian.competitive_landscape: Cross-Caspian movement today relies on infrequent ferries and energy-sector craft. A premium foiling tier would add speed and reliability the current options lack.
caspian.seasonality: The northern Caspian can ice in winter and the sea sees strong seasonal winds; scheduling follows the calm-water seasons.
caspian.regulatory_note: Caspian littoral states run national maritime registries and border-control regimes on an inland sea shared by five countries; cross-border legs (e.g. a trans-Caspian Baku crossing) require bilateral clearance, while intra-national coastal legs sit under each state's port authority. Early corridors are framed domestic-first, with cross-sea trunks sealed as clearances allow.

maghreb.tagline: Atlantic facades, Mediterranean bays, and the Strait of Gibraltar — North Africa's two-sea coast.
maghreb.summary: The Maghreb runs along two seas: Morocco's Atlantic facade from Tangier to Casablanca, Rabat and Agadir; and the Mediterranean coast that curves through Algeria's port cities — Algiers, Oran and Béjaïa — and Tunisia's Gulf of Tunis, Sahel marinas, and the islands of Kerkennah and Djerba. The Strait of Gibraltar at Tangier is one of the world's busiest passenger-sea crossings, ferry culture runs deep, and home-grown super-apps like Yassir already move daily mobility across these cities by phone. The premium water tier between marina, island and port city is the piece still missing.
maghreb.why_marine_mobility: North Africa faces the sea on almost every side, yet its coastal travel still runs on slow vehicle ferries, congested coast roads, and seasonal diesel fast-ferries. Morocco threads the Atlantic and the Mediterranean around the busy Strait of Gibraltar; Algeria's life concentrates in its Mediterranean port cities; and Tunisia rings a coast of bays, marinas and islands where the road is long and the sea is direct. A quiet, scheduled foiling tier turns those crossings — the Strait, the urban bays, the island shuttles — into the fast, clean leg they have never had.

demand_signals.label: The Strait of Gibraltar at scale
demand_signals.note: Tangier–Tarifa is one of the world's busiest passenger-sea crossings, with enormous summer volumes during the Marhaba diaspora movement and year-round trade — a short ~16 nm hop run today on large diesel fast-ferries.

demand_signals.label: Home-grown super-apps already at the curb
demand_signals.note: Yassir, born in Algeria, alongside platforms like Bolt and Careem, already moves daily ride-hailing across Maghreb cities — the water leg between port, marina and island is the natural premium extension of that habit.

demand_signals.label: Marina and island leisure coast
demand_signals.note: Tangier Marina, Casablanca, the Tunisian Sahel marinas of Port El Kantaoui and Monastir, and the islands of Kerkennah and Djerba anchor a growing Mediterranean resort and yachting economy built around arrival by water.

use_cases.title: The Strait and coastal commuter corridors
use_cases.body: Tangier–Tarifa and dense coastal corridors like Casablanca–Rabat and the Tunis bay carry heavy commuter and trade demand — exactly where a fast, scheduled foiling line beats both the road and the slow ferry.

use_cases.title: Marina-to-marina and resort hops
use_cases.body: Tangier's and Casablanca's urban bays, the Tunisian Sahel marinas of Port El Kantaoui and Monastir, and Algeria's port-city waterfronts turn a premium foiling transfer into part of the visit.

use_cases.title: Island shuttles upgraded
use_cases.body: The Kerkennah and Djerba island crossings, run today on slow vehicle ferries, are exactly the short legs a quiet, dry, zero-emission hydrofoil serves better.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The urban bays and island shuttles — the Tangier and Casablanca marina runs, the Gulf of Tunis hops, Sfax–Kerkennah and Jorf–Djerba — sit inside Pioneer II's all-electric ≤70 nm band, quiet and zero-emission off redeveloped marinas.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The exposed crossings and longer coastal trunks — the Strait of Gibraltar, the Atlantic Casablanca–Rabat–Agadir corridor, and cross-Mediterranean hops — extend into Quanta-LR's hybrid ≤700 nm range, where sea-keeping and range matter.

maghreb.transit_planning: For a Maghreb port authority or super-app: the coastline already carries heavy ferry and commuter traffic, and the digital mobility habit is already there. A foiling tier adds a fast, clean premium leg on the Strait, the urban bays, and the island crossings — without new road or rail.
maghreb.competitive_landscape: Today the coast splits between large diesel fast-ferries on the international Strait crossing, slow vehicle ferries to the islands, and congested coast roads and rail along the bays. None offers a fast, quiet, clean premium tier — exactly the empty middle electric-hydrofoil mobility fills.
maghreb.seasonality: The Strait peaks massively in summer with the Marhaba diaspora movement and runs year-round for trade; the Mediterranean bays, marinas and islands enjoy a long warm season (roughly April–October) with a calm, sheltered coast — so an operator can follow premium demand across the calendar.
